item.title: struggle together i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again. when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over. when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done befo...
item.description:
作者：Ryo Lu 账号：@ryolu_ 简介：Designed @Cursor_ai, @NotionHQ, @Stripe, built startups. I make a world where anyone can make software. Aspiring k-pop idol.
struggle together
i learned programming and design by trying, failing, and trying again.
when i hit a wall, i figured out how to climb it. read something i barely understood. took things apart. asked someone for help. started over.
when i began my career, i kept doing things i had never done before. trying different ways to make something work. when i stopped learning, i moved on to the next struggle.
many things i made weren’t very good. but after enough rounds, something stuck. what once took so much effort became part of how i thought. i could feel something was wrong before i knew how to explain it.
it became like water.
i think about what went into that. the bug i couldn’t fix. the design that looked right until someone used it. the conversation that made me realize my flaws.
now we can ask a machine.
i’ve made things with these tools that i might never have made otherwise. i don’t miss every tedious task. but i wonder what happens when we remove the difficulty before we understand what it was teaching us.
we ask. something appears. it works well enough. we move on.
we learn how to get results without necessarily understanding how it works. and because the result looks complete, it becomes easy to miss the questions we never learned to ask.
there is another side to this.
working with people is uncomfortable.
everyone wants something different. everyone has a history you don’t know. someone cares about a detail you think is unimportant. someone pushes back when you want to move. someone needs time when you feel certain.
it takes a while to find each other.
but sometimes, after struggling together, you become a band.
you know who notices what you miss. who can pull an idea apart without killing it. when to step in, when to slow down, when to let someone else carry the rhythm.
you share something unfinished. admit you don’t know. hurt each other, apologize, try again. eventually you make something none of you could have made alone.
some of my closest friendships came from working this way. smart, caring humans who saw me confused, wrong, tired, excited. people i could be vulnerable with. people whose ideas changed mine.
i worry we are making it easier to avoid that beginning.
an agent is always there. patient. ready to keep going. talking to it can feel easier than reaching toward someone who might misunderstand you, disagree, or have somewhere else to be.
sometimes that ease helps. but if we keep choosing it, where do the friendships begin?
i picture each of us with our own agents. our own explanations. our own little worlds. making more things, with fewer reasons to leave the screen or work through a difference with another person.
and these worlds aren’t entirely ours.
they run on machines in server farms, owned by companies, shaped by interests we may not see. we bring them our questions, our work, our loneliness. they become part of how we understand what is real.
is that freedom?
or a comfortable kind of confinement, where everything responds to us but fewer things reach us?
i don’t think pain makes something good. there are struggles nobody should have to endure. but i don’t want to lose the difficulty of learning something unfamiliar, or getting to know someone who isn’t like me.
maybe we need tools that help us spend more time with the world, instead of giving us fewer reasons to enter it. tools that make it easier to find people, share something unfinished, and work through what we couldn’t figure out alone.
sometimes i want to close the laptop.
sit with people i love. play something we haven’t figured out yet. miss a note, lose the rhythm, listen until we find each other again.
like a jazz band. everyone bringing something different. nobody knowing where we’ll end up.
i don’t want a life without struggle. i want people to struggle with. something we can feel, change, and make our own.
music we couldn’t have made alone, instead of the silent static of the server farm.

Large companies barely had the resources ...
item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
We’ll likely have 1,000X more tokens flowing through cyber agents soon than we do today.
As the surface area of cyber risk increases, at some point soon it will be nearly impossible to keep up with the volume of new risks (we’re essentially already there). Large companies barely had the resources to pull this off before, but the vast majority of companies don’t.
There’s a never ending set of libraries to keep up with, tools to leverage, and sprawling infrastructure and code to secure. We’ll have agent swarms that can fan out, leverage any security tool, test various perpetuations of attacks, read through logs, process enterprise data for risk level, and more.
This capability only emerged in the past few months. Wouldn’t have been possible before long running agents and computer use were good enough, and models hadn’t been trained on cyber deeply. That’s all changing now.
This is a huge area of opportunity right now for every layer of the security stack across identity, firewall, network, code scanning, data protection, and more. And it’s at least one reason to be optimistic about the balance of offensive and defensive capability.

作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
I oddly love the models' engineering vernacular: gate, evidence, culprit, durable, provenance, contract…
A lot of these stem from most engineering being debugging and understanding existing systems, where you take on the detective / auditor roles. You do forensics.
I wonder what the *minimum viable English* in fact is to be productive. ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English contains ~900 approved words. I suspect we need far fewer.

Of all the learning apps that my 4-year-old and I have tried, @once_reading is the only one that we’ve managed to persist in following for months.
It works because:
1. It builds a habit where you need to learn with your kid daily
2. It has lightweight gamification like taking a silly photo with your kid after every lesson
3. After 30 lessons, Once will send you books for your kid to read by themselves, giving them a big feeling of accomplishment
My kid loves reading now and will even choose her Once books over YouTube and the phone (sometimes at least) which is the highest compliment 😅
This is not sponsored or anything I just love the product.
Try out Once here: https://t.co/RbDiwACYbI

item.title: Jev: The AI That Makes Decisions, Not Text - and Why It Changes Everything (Diogo Almeida)
item.description:
播客：The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
Speaker 1 | 00:00 - 00:18 95% Einstein, 5% mister Bean. And if it doesn't tell you when it's the mister Bean, then how are you gonna automate anything? I wrote a document at OpenAI. We could have had AGI last year, and I still believe that to be true. Pre training is a giant dumpster fire of wasting resources.
Speaker 1 | 00:18 - 00:31 When I first started this project, I literally thought it would take a week. You can now express things that you couldn't express in software before. I think that the future will be unbelievably sci fi. We're building fraud, not god. Absolutely.
Speaker 2 | 00:31 - 00:53 That is Jogo Almeida, CEO of TypeSafe, the company behind JEV. A month ago, nobody had heard of JEV. Then he blanched, hit a nerve in the AI world, and quickly became the most copied model in AI. JEV is both fascinating and perplexing. It's a new kind of model and is clearly a big deal, yet even some AI insiders struggle to explain what it is while others dismiss it as just a classifier.
Speaker 2 | 00:53 - 01:07 So we went to the source and asked Diogo to walk us through JEV in plain English. What it is, where it's going, and why copycats are missing the point. I'm Matt Turk, and this is the BAT Podcast. Diogo, welcome.
Speaker 1 | 01:07 - 01:08 Thank you. Thank you. Hey.
Speaker 2 | 01:08 - 01:38 Alright. This is a super fun time, to be doing this conversation, in part because, just yesterday, I believe, as we were recording this, you guys announced, your gigantic series a, 870,000,000 series a at a 7,500,000,000 valuation. It's been a wild three weeks just looking at some stats. Your launch video had 40,000,000 views. Talked to somebody about a million users a day, a trillion tokens a day, a third of the Fortune five hundred.
Speaker 2 | 01:40 - 01:50 So, it it sounds like you're indeed building, what you call the Jivolution. I love the term. I'm just curious what it feels like from the inside.
Speaker 1 | 01:50 - 02:13 Where do I start? I will say that a lot of those stats don't really matter for what I feel like is the devolution. To me, I knew it would be happening when builders started playing with it and doing the weird stuff. And especially when people were starting to make apps that they maybe could have done before but didn't bother with because AI was so expensive. You know?
Speaker 1 | 02:13 - 02:42 I I... We push the boundaries of intelligence per second, but I think the future is going to be intelligence per dollar primarily. And I think really getting people to play with, like like, the idea that intelligence per dollar has dropped to orders of magnitude is what will make the Jevolution unstoppable independent of enterprise adoption, users, stats, whatever. To me, it's about people playing around with things and starting to... I can't think of a non corny way to say it, but, like, build the future.
Speaker 1 | 02:43 - 03:01 You know? Like like that to be used, the unstoppable energy. And no matter how big that initial snowball is, it will become gigantic. So, I've been celebrating this for something like two and a half weeks now. I've actually had to do soul searching because I think one of my big life goals has been achieved.
Speaker 1 | 03:02 - 03:11 And, yeah, the stats are obviously great. Growing fast is obviously great. I love that we are also getting a lot
Speaker 2 | 03:11 - 03:11 of
Speaker 1 | 03:11 - 03:25 the distribution that we knew we would get in two years, but much faster than we thought. These are all obviously phenomenal things. But the leading indicator of it all is builders being inspired to do new things.
Speaker 2 | 03:25 - 03:40 And just to, ask a couple of, like, the startup related questions. So you guys were in stealth for two years. I'm I'm curious how you thought about it in in a world where, like, everybody's on x every two minutes to talk about something. Why did you decide to be in stealth?
Speaker 1 | 03:40 - 04:01 No one's asked me that, so that's fun. I would say, I think, quite contrarianly. And I think that this whole AI has a gigantic overpromise under deliver issue. And, you know, I think people really saw that with our launch. Like, when we first launched the video, people were like, oh, that's fake.
Speaker 1 | 04:01 - 04:15 It's kind of interesting, but, like, there's no way it's true. The launch really picked off... Up when people started playing with it and showing their results. And I think that under promise, over deliver of our launch is what really made it take off. And it's been...
Speaker 1 | 04:16 - 04:43 I can't think of a launch in AI that has been under promise, over deliver since ChatGPT, so that might be why it took off. I'm not an expert in, like, social dynamics. So I really, really, you know, for better or for worse, I ignore the noise in the field and really focus on what I think is most important. And I just did not buy the story at all that AI was solving all sorts of problems. Because if you actually look at all the evidence, it's...
Speaker 1 | 04:44 - 04:52 AI is incredible and also incredibly underwhelming and that allowed me to really ignore all of the noise in the market.
Speaker 2 | 04:52 - 05:05 But, you know, doing this in obscurity while everybody's, you know, getting, celebrated, how do you keep a team energized and keep yourself energized building something sort of, you know, without anyone really knowing?
Speaker 1 | 05:05 - 05:15 I don't think that... I I... Maybe maybe the last couple of weeks have changed me. I hope not. I don't think I get really motivated by being celebrated on all of that.
Speaker 1 | 05:15 - 05:39 I actually had to do a lot of therapy just to be okay with being in our launch video because I actually, before all of this, enjoyed being in obscurity. Like, I'm a technologist through and through, I think. And what really motivated me for this is that there was clearly a gigantic technological gap. And it was clearly obvious no one was addressing it. So that was my...
Speaker 1 | 05:39 - 05:56 I I I never had any doubt. I... It was, even when I first had this idea long before I started the company, I wrote a document at OpenAI. We could have had AGI last year. And I still believe that to be true because a g...
Speaker 1 | 05:56 - 06:24 How OpenAI defines AGI is a very low bar, and the models are super fucking smart. Like like, we're we're not really putting those facts together, and I think a lot of the people who, like to commentate on the field just say like, oh, it's a distribution problem where that... That's obviously not the case if you pay attention to any, like, real world stuff. So I had very little doubts. I think that we managed to get a team like, you know, our team obviously doesn't care about, you know, that maybe there...
Speaker 1 | 06:24 - 06:48 There's a spectrum, but, like, our team is not driven by the hype cycles as well because if they were, they wouldn't have joined us. I think they really believed in our mission. Or if they didn't, you know, we had nontechnical people on the team. They really believed we had a bunch of, like, super smart people maybe they don't understand what the model is for but they're like holy crap these guys are cooking this is worth a bet so I don't think the team is that affected by it.
Speaker 2 | 06:48 - 07:18 Well what's funny is that I hear all of this and what's fascinating at the same time is that you guys need to seem to be kind of like natural born marketers and I'm sure you'll cringe out of the term, but, you know, you keep writing, you're tweeting very effectively, it sounds like you're doing this out of authenticity because you're so inspired by the mission and the rest follows. I'm trying to tease out, you know, lessons for for others, that would love to have, you know, a fraction of the success that, JEV had at at launch.
